questions.q: What must the first line of every teamcode file be?
questions.correct: A package line naming where the file lives
wrong: An @TeleOp label giving the program a name
A runOpMode method that runs the match
A telemetry line that prints a message
questions.explain: Every teamcode file starts with package org.firstinspires.ftc.teamcode; — it tells Java which folder the file belongs to. Imports, the class, and methods come after.

questions.correct: Pull in ready-made code your program needs
wrong: Delete code you no longer want to keep
Print messages onto the Driver Hub screen
Reverse the direction of a drive motor
questions.explain: import lines bring in classes someone already wrote (like LinearOpMode) so you can use them. The FTC library ships with lots of imports available.

questions.q: What does @TeleOp mark a program as?
questions.correct: A driver-controlled program, not an autonomous one
wrong: A program that only prints telemetry values
A file that cannot be run on the robot
The single fastest program on the whole robot
questions.explain: @TeleOp is a label (annotation) marking the program as tele-operated — driven by a human. It makes the program show up in the TeleOp list on the Driver Hub.

questions.correct: Start from FTC's blueprint and add your own parts
wrong: Make the program run twice as long as normal
Copy another team's already-finished robot program
Delete the parts of LinearOpMode you dislike
questions.explain: extends LinearOpMode means you inherit FTC's pre-built blueprint — which knows how to talk to the Driver Hub and wait for START — and build your own code on top of it.

questions.correct: A named set of steps you run by its name
wrong: A single number stored inside the robot
A wire that connects the hub to a motor
A label that names the whole program file
questions.explain: A method is a named recipe: a set of steps you can run by calling its name, like following a recipe in a cookbook. runOpMode is the main one.

questions.correct: The robot's main recipe that runs during a match
wrong: A helper method that only reverses one motor
A variable that counts the loops so far
The import that pulls in the FTC library
questions.explain: runOpMode() is the main method for a match. When you press START, the controller calls it, and everything your program does happens inside it.

questions.q: Which three parts does every runOpMode have?
questions.correct: Init once, waitForStart, then the run loop
wrong: Import, delete, then export the whole file
Build, charge, then unplug the battery
Score, reset, then charge the battery again
questions.explain: Every runOpMode has init (runs once at INIT), waitForStart() (pauses until START), and the run loop (while opModeIsActive(), ~50 times a second).

questions.correct: Pauses the program until START is pressed
wrong: Runs the loop code exactly one single time
Reverses all four drive motors at once
Prints the word "start" onto the telemetry
questions.explain: waitForStart() holds the program right after INIT and doesn't move on until the driver presses the START button on the Driver Hub.

questions.q: About how often does the run loop repeat?
wrong: Around once every 50 seconds
Exactly one time per whole match
Around 5000 times every second
questions.explain: while (opModeIsActive()) repeats roughly 50 times per second until the match ends — fast enough to feel instant to the driver.

questions.q: Code inside the run loop braces will...
questions.correct: Repeat every loop, about 50 times a second
wrong: Run one single time, then never run again
Only run during the autonomous phase
Run backward, from the bottom to the top
questions.explain: Anything inside the while (opModeIsActive()) braces repeats every loop. Code above the loop (in init) runs only once.

questions.q: What is a class, in plain terms?
questions.correct: A blueprint — the plan the file describes
wrong: A single button on the driver's controller
A number the robot stores between loops
A wire running from the hub to a motor
questions.explain: A class is a blueprint: the file is a plan. MecanumDrive is a class, and it describes how that program is built — like the plans for a building.

questions.correct: The match still running and not yet stopped
wrong: The battery being completely charged up
The code having no missing semicolons
The robot sitting perfectly still and quiet
questions.explain: opModeIsActive() returns true while the match is live and STOP hasn't been pressed. When it turns false, the loop ends and the program finishes.

questions.q: Where does code that should run only once go?
questions.correct: In the init part, before waitForStart()
wrong: Inside the run loop's curly braces
In a separate exported zip file
After the class's final closing brace
questions.explain: One-time setup (like finding motors) goes in init, before waitForStart(). Loop code, which repeats, goes inside the while (opModeIsActive()) braces.

questions.q: What usually causes a build to fail on a single line?
questions.correct: A missing semicolon at the end of the line
wrong: Writing the code in all capital letters
Leaving one blank line between two methods
Naming a variable with a very long word
questions.explain: A missing semicolon is a classic build breaker — Java expects one at the end of most statements. Type mismatches are the other common cause.

questions.q: Why does your program start from LinearOpMode?
questions.correct: It already knows how to talk to the Driver Hub
wrong: It makes the drive motors spin much faster
It is required in order to score any points
It stores the robot's position on the field
questions.explain: LinearOpMode is FTC's ready-made blueprint that handles talking to the Driver Hub and waiting for START. You extend it so you don't have to write all that yourself.
